content: Children, similar to adults, are required to fast before undergoing general anesthesia. The primary purpose of this fasting is to reduce both the volume and acidity of the stomach contents. This reduction is believed to lower the risk of regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents during surgical procedures. Historically, the standard fasting protocol has been nil-by-mouth from midnight, but recent advancements have led to the consideration of more lenient fasting regimens. However, the adoption of these updated practices has been slow, largely due to uncertainties regarding the optimal fasting duration and the type and quantity of intake that should be allowed. The objective of this review was to systematically evaluate the effects of various preoperative fasting regimens, including differences in fasting duration, the type of intake permitted, and the volume of intake allowed. The review also aimed to assess the impact of these regimens on perioperative complications and the overall well-being of pediatric patients. Specific outcomes of interest included aspiration, regurgitation, associated morbidity, thirst, hunger, pain, comfort, behavior, nausea, and vomiting. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, EBSCO CINAHL, and the National Research Register. The search also included conference proceedings, reference lists of articles, and consultations with experts in the field. The search was completed up to June 2009. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials focusing on preoperative fasting regimens in children were identified for inclusion. Data extraction and quality assessment of the trials were performed independently by three authors. Additional information, including details on adverse events, was obtained by contacting the authors of the included studies. This updated review identified two additional eligible studies, bringing the total number of included studies to 25. These studies encompassed 47 randomized controlled comparisons involving 2,543 children who were considered to be at normal risk of regurgitation or aspiration during anesthesia. The review found only one reported case of aspiration and regurgitation across all included studies. Importantly, children who were allowed to consume clear fluids up to 120 minutes before surgery did not exhibit higher gastric volumes or lower gastric pH levels compared to those who adhered to prolonged fasting. Furthermore, children permitted to drink fluids preoperatively experienced less thirst and hunger, demonstrated better behavior, and reported greater comfort compared to those who fasted for extended periods. The consumption of clear fluids prior to surgery did not result in clinically significant differences in gastric volume or pH. However, evidence regarding the preoperative intake of milk was limited. Additionally, the volume of fluid consumed during the preoperative period did not appear to influence intraoperative gastric volume or pH. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to suggest that children who are denied oral fluids for more than six hours before surgery derive any benefit in terms of intraoperative gastric volume or pH compared to children who are allowed to consume unlimited clear fluids up to two hours before surgery. Allowing children to drink fluids preoperatively provides a more comfortable experience by alleviating thirst and hunger. These findings are applicable only to children who are considered to be at normal risk of aspiration or regurgitation during anesthesia.
